look_here_first: SILKY BLUESTEM (introduced): LOOK HERE FIRST for a tight, densely white-silky cluster of terminal racemes, then trace the entire flowering culm to its base. A white-bearded TRUE STEM NODE is shared with Kleberg and some native bluestems, not proof of silky. Inspect an attached sessile fertile spikelet beside its pedicelled sterile companion, the lower glume's transverse subapical hair fringe and the fertile-lemma awn. Texas plants may differ from the photographed Australian forms; do not infer subspecies, native status or species ID from color or one detached head.

Ten Learner panels = nine EXACT silky-bluestem Australian photos, one clearly DIFFERENT Kleberg node comparison. best_field_traits: Native to Australia (and other Old World regions) but INTRODUCED in Texas; an Australian-source photograph does not make it a native Texas restoration species.
Often tight tufted grass with white-silvery densely hairy fingerlike racemes, commonly 2–6 but broad variation among authorities.
Bearded TRUE CULM NODES; a dense white ring is visible in exact-species licensed photos. NOT unique to Kleberg.
Subsessile/sessile flowering racemes in some floras, compared with the conspicuously stalked subdigitate arrangement of Kleberg; overlapping counts and growth stages need botanical review.
Sessile spikelets commonly ~3–4.5 mm, glume near apex showing distinct transverse fringe of hairs; matched actual macro still needed.
Non-native in Texas, so exclude it from native restoration seed mixes.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full flowering head with count of racemes against ruler
A mature spikelet pair; sterile companion glume hair vs fertile awn
Node hair sheath and stem; true collar ligule
Base to document tuft/rhizome not inferred from hand-held sample
crew_field_check: Start from whole rooted plant to establish growth form.
Photograph flowering head and collar on same individual.
Use hand-lens/25x macro to measure floret structure when needed; photos without it support only provisional source determination.
No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.

measured_reproductive_key_20261024.growth_form: Introduced warm-season tufted perennial in the standard D. sericeum treatment; Kew GrassBase gives erect culms 30–80 cm and blades 8–15 cm × 2–4 mm. Treat subspecies or unusual annual variants as unresolved, not a local identification.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.true_ligule_and_collar: At the ACTUAL blade–sheath junction look for an eciliate membranous ligule about 1 mm (Kew GrassBase), versus 1–2 mm in VicFlora's subsp. sericeum account; the conspicuous white bearded hair ring belongs to a separate CULM NODE, not the ligule.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.flowering_architecture: Kew GrassBase: 1–6 digitate/subdigitate white-villous racemes 4–7 cm long; broader Kew flora account allows 1–15 racemes. Count complete attached racemes, not detached wisps. Lowest 1–6 pairs may be male or sterile, not ordinary fertile pairs.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.paired_spikelets: At a rachis joint expect a fertile SESSILE spikelet and a PEDICELLED sterile companion. AusGrass gives sessile fertile spikelet 4–4.5 mm and pedicelled companion 3–5 mm; the sterile companion contains an empty lemma, not a second awned grain.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.glumes: Sessile LOWER glume flattened, several-nerved (AusGrass 5–8; VicFlora subsp. sericeum 7–11), with tubercle-based marginal cilia and a conspicuous TRANSVERSE SUBAPICAL hair fringe; UPPER glume narrower, keeled, about 3-nerved. Published nerve counts depend on taxon treatment and subspecies; do not infer subspecies or Texas provenance from these ranges.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.lemmas_and_awn: Lower floret sterile with a thin hyaline lemma; upper fertile lemma much reduced/stipitate, without palea in Kew treatment, and bears ONE dark bent/twisted awn approximately 25–32 mm (AusGrass) or about 30 mm (Kew). The conspicuous awn arises from the FERTILE LEMMA, not the glume or sterile pedicelled spikelet.
measured_reproductive_key_20261024.scale_and_scope: These are published botanical dimensions, not measurements from the three archived source photographs. Confirm mature spikelet parts at 10–30× with 1-mm scale. Australian photographs are not vouchers for Hays County or proof of a particular infraspecific taxon.

comparisons.key_distinctions: White bearded culm nodes are SHARED with Kleberg and many native cane bluestems. Silky usually has densely villous relatively more sessile flowering racemes and a glume subapical ciliate fringe; Kleberg commonly more stalked subdigitate racemes, with basal sterile/unawned pairs. A mature source-verified spikelet pair and attached full head is the only secure species-level test when silhouettes overlap.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Introduced SILKY BLUESTEM (not a native Texas bluestem). Examine the silvery-hairy flowering head and narrow, often paired racemes, and then magnify the companion sterile/pedicelled spikelet against the awned sessile fertile spikelet. Compare the basal clump and hairy stem nodes against invasive Kleberg bluestem. This photo shows only one small silky head held against fingers, not definitive spikelet dissection.
field_id_finish_pass.photographic_evidence: Source photograph shows a small narrow silver hairy flowering axis held before grassland; the photograph does NOT show legible spikelet glume hairs, true collar, or roots.
remaining_macro_photo_targets: True same-plant fertile and sterile paired spikelet glume hairs (1-mm ruler)
Flowering stalk/peduncle comparison with D. annulatum on matched mature specimens
Hays or Texas documented root base and collar; no county-native assertion
field_id_finish_pass.lookalikes: Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) usually has more clearly 2–15 fingerlike racemes and prominently WHITE-RINGED stem nodes, sometimes a creeping/stoloniferous base. D. sericeum's densely silky hair and narrow racemes are useful orientation cues, NOT decisive alone; mature spikelet, paired sterile companion, node and root base necessary. Both species introduced in Texas.
field_id_finish_pass.new_photographic_evidence: Two public licensed Australian photos verify live full tuft and dense white node hair ring; genus comparisons updated.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261024.LOOK_HERE_FIRST: SILKY BLUESTEM: find a densely silky, usually clustered fingerlike flowering head on a tufted grass. Check the true culm node (white beard is SHARED with Kleberg), then magnify an attached ~4–4.5 mm sessile fertile spikelet and ~3–5 mm sterile pedicelled partner. On the sessile LOWER glume seek the transverse subapical hair fringe; trace the single bent/twisted ~25–32 mm awn to its reduced fertile lemma. Never separate Silky/Kleberg/KR by silver color or a white node ring alone.
crew_sequence: 1. Trace an entire living culm to a rooted tuft and record perennial habit; no assumption from a hand-held head.
2. Photograph the complete digitate raceme cluster, count attached branches, and show whether their stalks are sessile/subsessile or conspicuously pedunculate.
3. Photograph a true hairy STEM NODE separately from an opened blade–sheath COLLAR; measure the approximately 1–2 mm membranous ligule with a 1-mm ruler.
4. At 10–30× locate one intact mature SESSILE+PEDICELLED spikelet pair and measure each independently.
5. Dissect sessile lower and upper glumes; photograph the lower glume's subapical ciliate arch and veins, then separate the sterile lower lemma and tiny awned fertile upper lemma.
6. Measure the complete bent/twisted awn from its fertile-lemma insertion, and inspect basal sterile/male pairs before making a species-level determination.
7. Compare same-scale D. annulatum (Kleberg) and Bothriochloa ischaemum (KR); uncertain plants stay bluestem sp. pending measured paired-spikelet evidence.

local_lookalikes.contrast: Also introduced; also may have long white hairs at true stem nodes and fingered heads. More clearly pedunculate/subdigitate heads and basal sterile pairs can help, but overlap. Compare mature lower-glume marginal hair pattern and paired spikelets; no single hairy node is decisive.

Introduced; clustered terminal racemes also overlap. Inspect papilla-based upper-blade hairs, node, paired spikelets and glume hair pattern on matched attached material. No species ID from head color.
Native cane bluestem can have a conspicuously hairy node too. Trace its full flowering architecture and attached spikelet pairs before any invasive-removal decision.

NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: Texas-vouchered rooted flowering tuft showing whole raceme insertion and a true culm node; include centimeter ruler, not a detached Australian head.
Same plant opened true blade–sheath collar with 1-mm ruler resolving the membranous ligule; do not label the hairy stem-node ring as ligule.
Attached mature fertile sessile + sterile pedicelled spikelet pair at 10–30×, 1-mm ruler, with glume and fertile-lemma awn attachment legible.
Separated sessile lower glume in face and edge views, calibrated subapical ciliate fringe and glume veins; actual sterile and fertile lemmas and bent awn base.
Matched mature D. sericeum / D. annulatum / KR and native cane comparison photos with specimen provenance and similar scales.
NEEDS_SITE_QA: Verify actual physical JPEG bytes, taxon/source attribution and per-image public reuse, retaining the existing CC BY-NC and CC BY 2.0 records unchanged.
Review existing gross-feature arrows against the displayed JPEG pixels; do not add microscopic glume, ligule or lemma arrows until visible and confirmed.
Verify public learner renders the physically archived photos and exact species comparisons; no Pages build or deployment is claimed in this species-only lane.
Keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until decisive attached pair, true collar and glume fringe are actually photographed, licensed, annotated and rendered.

4 · WHOLE HABIT: panel 1 is Australian source-labelled growing bunch, ROOTS NOT EXPOSED; do not infer perennial life cycle of a Texas introduction from this one image.

5 · COMPLETE HEAD: NEW panel 4 is actual Harry Rose CC BY 2.0 source-authenticated densely silky flowerhead with long dark projecting bent awns; original source external, NOT archived as an additional JPEG.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SILKY FINGERS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Real silky racemes + dark awns photographed; actual Texas subspecies unverified
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look at archived Australian panels 1 (source-identified living flowering tuft with roots hidden) and 4 (attached densely silky racemes and long dark awns). GrassBase describes about 1–6 racemes commonly 4–7 cm long, but broader floras and infraspecific forms overlap Kleberg. Australian photographs demonstrate habit, NOT a verified Texas subspecies or rooted local voucher. Do not rely on silvery color, raceme number or a bearded node alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE AUTHENTIC HEAD/HABIT PHOTOS — TX SAME-VOUCHER ROOTED FORM MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · BEARDED NODE VS LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Hairy TRUE stem node is shared; inner ligule is a tiny membrane.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual source-labelled silky bluestem NODE hair-ring photograph (panel 0) clearly shows a white beard around the true upright stem joint; panel 2 is DIFFERENT introduced Kleberg bluestem with a similar bearded node. The newly presented local CC BY 2.0 leaf/sheath image (panel 3) instead shows the blade and cylindrical sheath on the stem. Its two new gross arrows do NOT mark the true INNER ligule. AusGrass describes an ECILIATE membranous ligule about 0.5–1 mm (VicFlora subsp. sericeum ~1–2 mm): photograph the actual free membrane edge with 1-mm ruler, separate from the MUCH LONGER nodal beard and side hairs. Never treat beard presence alone as species proof.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE INNER LIGULE MEMBRANE NOW PHOTOGRAPHED (panel 5), still no 1-mm reference or local Texas voucher

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · ROOTED TUFT AND RACEME INSERTION
field_id_short_tiles.short: Australian tuft is context, not proof of Texas annual/perennial subspecies
field_id_short_tiles.details: The Australian whole-habit (panel 1, LOCALLY ARCHIVED) and local true sheath photo (panel 3) together support a bunching growth lesson, but NONE shows visibly exposed actual roots, crown-to-head physical continuity or possible short belowground rhizomes. Kew's broader descriptions call many perennial forms caespitose with occasional short rhizomes, while AusGrass distinguishes annual subsp. humilius from perennial subsp. sericeum. A Texas photographed individual could therefore differ in life cycle from the perennial Australian model. Rooted local same-voucher specimen, actual lower tiller connections and intact attached head required.
field_id_short_tiles.status: IN-SITU BUNCHED HABIT PARTIAL; TRUE ROOTED CROWN AND TEXAS ID MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · TWO DIFFERENT SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Measure a 4–4.5 mm sessile fertile spikelet beside a 3–5 mm pedicelled sterile one.
field_id_short_tiles.details: In the actual licensed Australian head image (panel 4), densely silky flowering branches, visible long brown awns and spikelet-bearing rachis are source-authenticated. But the tiny individual sessile fertile spikelet and adjacent pedicelled sterile companion, plus 2–6 basal sterile pairs, cannot be independently measured from those pixels. AusGrass describes fertile sessile ~4–4.5 mm and sterile pedicelled ~3–5 mm (depending infraspecific treatment). The taxon must be dissected at 10–30× and photographed with a physical 1-mm scale; apparent strand/awn position alone is insufficient.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-IDENTIFIED SPIKELET PAIR + SEPARATE SESSILE/PEDICELLED REAL SCALE PHOTOS ADDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · GLUME FRINGE, LEMMAS AND AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Find the lower glume's transverse hair fringe and one bent fertile-lemma awn.
field_id_short_tiles.details: This photographed head shows pale hairs and long stiff awns as broad morphology, but individual LOWER GLUME transverse subapical ciliary arch and BOTH glume surfaces are too small/hidden for true anatomical annotation. AusGrass keys subsp. humilius (~4-mm spikelet, 5–7-veined lower glume, often raceme shorter than 4 cm, annual) against subsp. sericeum (~4.5 mm, 9–10-veined, usually >4-cm raceme, perennial). These ranges are PUBLISHED, not yet demonstrated for any Texas voucher or the Australian photo. Isolate the actual sessile lower glume, its transverse hair line, attached awned fertile upper lemma, separate pedicelled sterile partner, and mm bar from the SAME specimen.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL DISSECTED REPRODUCTIVE UNIT ADDED; EXACT FERTILE LEMMA/AWN ORIGIN STILL UNLABELLED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · DON'T CONFUSE SILKY, KLEBERG AND NATIVES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Photographs support node/sheath/head; no measured pair or certified Texas subspecies
field_id_short_tiles.details: The five-panel lesson has FOUR source-identified silky-bluestem photographs: 0 (bearded true node), 1 (Australian living flowering tuft), 3 (blade/sheath; true inner ligule not exposed), and 4 (attached silky awned head). Panel 2 is explicitly DIFFERENT SPECIES Kleberg bluestem. The separately archived Melissa Walsh CC BY-NC original is not in this five-panel gallery. Both introduced Dichanthium species can have white-bearded nodes; KR and native cane bluestems also overlap in gross flowering appearance. Compare Texas rooted base, actual collar, complete raceme insertion and same-specimen mature sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair, lower-glume transverse subapical hair fringe and lemma awn origin. Preserve uncertain identifications and native look-alikes.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — NINE OPEN-LICENSE EXACT PHOTOS, ONE DIFFERENT-SPECIES COMPARISON, TX ROOTED CROWN STILL MISSING
